precepts.text: And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law. You see? A devout man according to the law. The other nations didn't have the law.
precepts.point: If y'all wasn't in Bishop Kani's class, it's called Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common, maybe two months ago. He goes really slow on it and it's excellent.

note.label: Raising Up the Tabernacle of David That Fell

precepts.why:
Cornelius is called “A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway.” How do you become a devout man? People go, yeah, he was another nation, but he was devout. No, no, no.

Look at how the scripture uses the word: “And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, having a good report of all the Jews which dwelt there”. You see? A devout man according to the law. The other nations did not have the law.

So how was Cornelius a devout man according to the law? How did he fear God? How did he know how to pray to God? He had to know the law. He even kept the hours of prayer: the angel came to him “about the ninth hour of the day”, and he told Peter, “at the ninth hour I prayed in my house”.

So yes, Cornelius is an Israelite, northern kingdom. His devotion was devotion to the law of God, which was given to Israel and to no other nation.

precepts.text: What does devout mean? Ananias was a devout man according to the law, having a good report. So when Acts 10 says Cornelius was a devout man, he was a law abiding man; he kept the laws of God.
precepts.point: A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway. His prayers and his alms came up for a memorial before God, and the angel told him to send men to Joppa and call for Simon, whose surname is Peter.

note.label: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.why:
Cornelius is called “A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house”. What does it mean to be devout? Acts 22 shows it: “And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, having a good report of all the Jews which dwelt there”. To be devout is to be devout according to the law, and to have a good report for it.

So when Acts 10 says Cornelius was a devout man, it is saying he was a law-abiding man. He kept the laws of God. He feared God with all his house, gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway.

His own messengers tell Peter the same thing later in the chapter: “Cornelius the centurion, a just man, and one that feareth God, and of good report among all the nation of the Jews”. The same good report Ananias had among the Jews, Cornelius had too.

That is why Peter came to understand that the vision was about man, not food, and that he should not call any man common or unclean. Cornelius was a just man and a devout man, a keeper of the law. “God is no respecter of persons: But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.”

precepts.text: Paul was brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers.
precepts.point: When men believe the law is done away they hold no morals to restrain them, and will put the teachers to death thinking they do the will of the Most High.

note.label: Acts 5: All Things Common, and We Ought to Obey God Rather Than Men

precepts.why:
Who was Gamaliel? Paul says, “I am verily a man which am a Jew, born in Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, yet brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers, and was zealous toward God, as ye all are this day.”

Gamaliel was a Pharisee and a doctor of the law, had in reputation among all the people, and Paul was brought up at his feet in the perfect manner of the law of the fathers. That is the man who stood up in the council and had the apostles put outside a little space.

precepts.text: Ananias is called a devout man according to the law, having a good report of all the Jews; that is the measure of the devout men who buried Stephen.
precepts.point: Devout men carried Stephen to his burial and made great lamentation over him. A devout man is a man according to the laws of the Most High who has a good report.

note.label: Acts 8: The Word Scattered Abroad, and the Baptism unto the Conscience

precepts.why:
“devout men carried Stephen to his burial, and made great lamentation over him.” What is a devout man? Ananias gives the measure: “a devout man according to the law, having a good report of all the Jews which dwelt there”. A devout man is a man according to the laws of the Most High who has a good report.

So the men who buried Stephen and lamented over him were men of the law with a good report among the Jews.

precepts.text: Paul gives his own account: a Jew born in Tarsus, brought up at the feet of Gamaliel, taught according to the perfect manner of the law and zealous toward the Most High, and he persecuted this way unto the death, binding both men and women.
precepts.point: Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word. Because of the great persecution the disciples had to flee, and our fathers were fugitives, always on the run, the way it was done to men like Nat Turner. It is going to come to that point again, where a brother might have to house a teacher whose name is on the news, wanted for sedition; you might be charged as guilty by association, but you have to see past it to protect your brother, because the gospel has to go forward. This is why we need such a high level of unity and love for one another to survive.

note.label: Acts 8: The Word Scattered Abroad, and the Baptism unto the Conscience

precepts.why:
Paul gives his own account of who was doing the scattering: “I am verily a man which am a Jew, born in Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, yet brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers, and was zealous toward God, as ye all are this day. And I persecuted this way unto the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women.”

A Jew, taught the law in its perfect manner under Gamaliel and zealous toward the Most High, and with that zeal he persecuted this way unto the death, binding both men and women. This is the persecution that scattered the disciples abroad, and it is what our fathers went through as fugitives, always on the run.

precepts.text: Paul's own retelling: those with him saw the light and were afraid but heard not the voice, the other half of the same account.
precepts.point: It was a caravan of men. Based on each man's account, one group heard the voice but saw no man, and another group saw the light but heard no voice, just as men running from the same scene report different pieces of it. There is no contradiction in the Bible.
precepts.why:
People read Acts 9:7 against Paul's own retelling in Acts 22 and claim a contradiction. Here the men “stood speechless, hearing a voice, but seeing no man.” There Paul says, “they that were with me saw indeed the light, and were afraid; but they heard not the voice of him that spake to me.” There is no contradiction.

It was a caravan of men. Based on each man's account, one group heard the voice but saw no man, and another group saw the light but heard no voice, just as men running from the same scene report different pieces of it. Acts 22 is the other half of the same account: “suddenly there shone from heaven a great light round about me”, Saul fell to the ground and heard the voice say, “Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?”, and the answer, “I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom thou persecutest.” There is no contradiction in the Bible.

precepts.text: Paul was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel, taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers.
precepts.point: Ananias enters, lays his hands on him as "Brother Saul," and immediately something like scales fall from his eyes, he receives sight, and is baptized. Paul was not taught by Peter or the other apostles; Christ himself taught him directly.
precepts.why:
Paul was “brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers, and was zealous toward God”. Under Gamaliel he was taught the law of the fathers in its perfect manner.

But the gospel he was not taught by Peter or the other apostles. When Ananias laid hands on him and the scales fell from his eyes, it was Christ himself, who appeared to him in the way, who taught him directly.

precepts.text: Tarsus, Paul's birthplace, is a city in Cilicia, modern-day Mersin, Turkey.
precepts.point: Saul speaks boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus and disputes against the Grecians, but they go about to slay him, so the brethren bring him down to Caesarea and send him to Tarsus. Caesarea sits on the coast of Israel bordering the region of Syria near Damascus.
precepts.why: Paul is “a Jew, born in Tarsus, a city in Cilicia”. Tarsus, where the brethren sent him, was his birthplace, a city in Cilicia, modern-day Mersin, Turkey. When the Grecians went about to slay him, the brethren sent him home.

precepts.text: The chief captain asks Paul, "Art thou a Roman?" and Paul says yes, though he is an Israelite, because Roman is his citizenship, not his race.
precepts.point: Because the Israelites were scattered through every province and took the names of their captivities, scholars cannot tell a Roman Jewish soldier from a Roman by his name alone, and the New Testament was written in Greek because Israel spoke Greek under the Greeks. Correcting a misheard reference to Luke 3, the centurions of scripture were often Israelite servants in the army.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:
“Then the chief captain came, and said unto him, Tell me, art thou a Roman? He said, Yea.”

Paul is an Israelite, and still he says yes, because Roman is his citizenship, not his race. The Israelites were scattered through every province and took the names of their captivities, so scholars cannot tell a Roman Jewish soldier from a Roman by his name alone. The New Testament was written in Greek because Israel spoke Greek under the Greeks.

So a centurion of the Italian band with a Latin name like Cornelius can be an Israelite. The centurions of scripture were often Israelite servants in the army.

precepts.text: Ananias is called "a devout man according to the law," so devout is always measured by keeping the law.
precepts.point: Scholars themselves suppose from this language that Cornelius was a Jew or a proselyte instructed in the Jewish religion, because the pagan Romans worshipped the sun, the moon, and gods like Mars, Venus, Jupiter, and Hermes, not the commandments.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:
Cornelius was “A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway.” To be devout is to be devout according to the law, a man who keeps the commandments.

Scripture measures it that way: “one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, having a good report of all the Jews which dwelt there.” Devout is always measured by keeping the law. So when Cornelius is called devout, he is being called a keeper of the commandments.

precepts.text: Ananias, a devout man according to the law, having a good report of all the Jews, showing "devout" means law-keeping.
precepts.point: To fear him and work righteousness means to keep the commandments; "devout" means to keep the law of the Most High.

note.label: Acts 11: The Gentiles Are Scattered Israel

precepts.why:
“And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, having a good report of all the Jews which dwelt there.”

Devout means to keep the law of the Most High. Cornelius was called devout, and a devout man is devout according to the law.

precepts.text: Paul confesses he persecuted "this way" unto the death, binding men and women into prisons.
precepts.point: Before the followers of Christ were called Christians in Antioch, they were called "this way."

note.label: Acts 11: The Gentiles Are Scattered Israel

precepts.why:
Paul confessed it: “And I persecuted this way unto the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women.”

The same Saul who persecuted this way was the one Barnabas went to Tarsus to seek and brought to Antioch, where “a whole year they assembled themselves with the church, and taught much people.” And there the way was first called Christians.

precepts.point: He called himself the chief of sinners. 2 Corinthians 12:7 says a thorn in the flesh was given to him, the messenger of Satan, lest he be exalted above measure.

note.label: Galatians 1: Paul's Apostleship and the True Gospel

precepts.why:
Paul tells how he profited above his equals: “I am verily a man which am a Jew, born in Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, yet brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers, and was zealous toward God, as ye all are this day.”

Brought up at the feet of Gamaliel and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers: that is the zeal of the traditions of his fathers he speaks of in Galatians. Paul was close to being perfect, but he battled just like we battle.
